1	\section{Introduction}
2	\label{sec:introduction}
3	
4	Training-free\footnote{We use ``training-free'' and ``zero-shot'' interchangeably to denote prompting without parameter updates.}\footnote{Code and data will be released upon acceptance. Anonymous review materials: \url{https://anonymous.4open.science/r/schema-dag-extraction}} LLM information extraction---prompting a large language model with a target schema and asking it to extract structured information without any task-specific fine-tuning---enables rapid deployment across new domains and ontologies. This zero-shot paradigm eliminates the need for labeled data, making it attractive for applications where annotation is expensive or schemas evolve frequently \cite{llm4ie-survey-2024}. Yet the paradigm carries a critical limitation: performance degrades sharply as the number of candidate types in the prompt schema grows. On named entity recognition, recall drops from 0.72 with a single candidate type to a plateau of ${\sim}$0.27 across intermediate schema sizes (22--44 types) before partial recovery at full-schema. On relation extraction, accuracy falls from 85.7\% with one relation to 50.4\% with 80 relations (sentence-level) and from 88.0\% to 38.7\% with 96 relations (document-level)---near or exceeding halving. This degradation is not academic: real-world ontologies routinely define 50--200+ types, placing them squarely in the regime where training-free extraction becomes unreliable.
5	
6	What explains this degradation? Prior decomposition strategies \cite{uniner-2024,llm-pee-2025,parse-2025} conflate two mechanisms: having more types to discriminate among (count) and having semantically similar types to confuse (confusability) (hereafter Channel~1 and Channel~2). None isolates which factor predicts the gains (\S\ref{sec:related_work}).
7	
8	We ask three questions. \textbf{RQ1}: Does type confusability independently predict extraction degradation beyond the effect of type count? \textbf{RQ2}: Through what

# FewRel data (3 seeds)
fewrel_seeds = {

}

# Few-NERD data (3 seeds)
fewnerd_seeds = {
    2:  {'s42': (0.5267, 0.1905), 's123': (0.4460, 0.1984), 's456': (0.5528, 0.1402)},
    6:  {'s42': (0.3899, 0.1153), 's123': (0.4217, 0.1341), 's456': (0.4092, 0.1197)},
    12: {'s42': (0.3057, 0.1017), 's123': (0.3568, 0.1119), 's456': (0.3051, 0.1050)},
    22: {'s42': (0.2684, 0.1029), 's123': (0.2768, 0.0905), 's456': (0.2577, 0.0922)},
    44: {'s42': (0.3007, 0.1116), 's123': (0.2724, 0.1146), 's456': (0.2898, 0.1366)},
    66: {'s42': (0.4071, 0.0017), 's123': (0.4067, 0.0014), 's456': (0.4067, 0.0016)},
}

print('=== FewRel Grand Means ===')
fewrel_grand = {}
fewrel_max_delta = 0
for count, seeds in sorted(fewrel_seeds.items()):
    means = [seeds['s42'][0], seeds['s123'][0], seeds['s456'][0]]
    stds = [seeds['s42'][1], seeds['s123'][1], seeds['s456'][1]]
    grand_mean = np.mean(means)
    avg_std = np.mean(stds)
    delta = max(means) - min(means)
    fewrel_max_delta = max(fewrel_max_delta, delta)
    fewrel_grand[count] = {'mean': grand_mean, 'std': avg_std}
    print(f'  count={count:2d}: grand_mean={grand_mean:.4f}, avg_std={avg_std:.4f}, seed_delta={delta:.4f}')

print(f'\n  FewRel max Delta across seeds: {fewrel_max_delta:.4f} = {fewrel_max_delta*100:.1f} pp')

print('\n=== Few-NERD Grand Means ===')
fewnerd_grand = {}
fewnerd_max_delta = 0
for count, seeds in sorted(fewnerd_seeds.items()):
    means = [seeds['s42'][0], seeds['s123'][0], seeds['s456'][0]]
    stds = [seeds['s42'][1], seeds['s123'][1], seeds['s456'][1]]
    grand_mean = np.mean(means)
    avg_std = np.mean(stds)
    delta = max(means) - min(means)
    fewnerd_max_delta = max(fewnerd_max_delta, delta)
    fewnerd_grand[count] = {'mean': grand_mean, 'std': avg_std}
    print(f'  count={count:2d}: grand_mean={grand_mean:.4f}, avg_std={avg_std:.4f}, seed_delta={delta:.4f}')

print(f'\n  Few-NERD max Delta across seeds: {fewnerd_max_delta:.4f} = {fewnerd_max_delta*100:.1f} pp')

# Overall max delta
overall_max = max(fewrel_max_delta, fewnerd_max_delta)
print(f'\n=== Overall max Delta: {overall_max:.4f} = {overall_max*100:.1f} pp ===')

# Key numbers for text
print(f'\n=== Key Numbers for Text ===')
print(f'FewRel count=4 grand mean: {fewrel_grand[4][\"mean\"]:.2f}')
print(f'FewRel count=80 grand mean: {fewrel_grand[80][\"mean\"]:.2f}')
print(f'Few-NERD count=2 grand mean: {fewnerd_grand[2][\"mean\"]:.2f}')
print(f'Few-NERD count=22 grand mean: {fewnerd_grand[22][\"mean\"]:.2f}')
print(f'Few-NERD count=44 grand mean: {fewnerd_grand[44][\"mean\"]:.2f}')
print(f'Few-NERD count=66 grand mean: {fewnerd_grand[66][\"mean\"]:.2f}')
print(f'Few-NERD plateau (mean of 22,44): {(fewnerd_grand[22][\"mean\"]+fewnerd_grand[44][\"mean\"])/2:.2f}')
"

tool_args.old_string: Figure~\ref{fig:main_results}a shows RE accuracy declines monotonically with schema size (0.87$\to$0.50 for FewRel). NER recall declines through intermediate counts (0.53$\to$0.27, plateauing across counts 22--44) before partial recovery at full-schema (0.41), where the elimination of type-filtering overhead restores extraction performance. DocRED replicates the monotonic RE pattern (88.0\%$\to$38.7\%, $-$56\%; Appendix). MAVEN exhibits a reversed trend attributable to centrality confounding (\S\ref{sec:centrality_confound}). The effect replicates on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct ($-$43\,pp on Few-NERD; per-batch $r = 0.725$; Table~\ref{tab:cross_model}), indicating schema configuration rather than model-specific factors predicts difficulty. The pattern replicates across seeds (42, 123; max $\Delta = 2.7$\,pp, within 1\,SD); intra-batch variance exceeds inter-seed variance by ${>}$5$\times$ at every count level (Appendix~\ref{app:variance-decomposition}). Formal trend analysis confirms monotonic RE decline (Jonckheere-Terpstra $J = 109{,}707$, $p < 0.001$, pooled across three seeds). Count curves (25 batches per level) establish trend direction with error bars; magnitude estimation relies on the higher-powered BCS-controlled experiments (\S\ref{sec:bcs_controlled}).
